{{Short description|Mathematical concept for comparing objects}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''partial equivalence relation''' (often abbreviated as '''PER''', in older literature also called '''restricted equivalence relation'''<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Scott |first1=Dana |title=Data Types as Lattices |journal=SIAM Journal on Computing |date=September 1976 |volume=5 |issue=3 |page=560 |doi=10.1137/0205037}}</ref>) is a [[homogeneous binary relation]] that is [[symmetric relation|symmetric]] and [[transitive relation|transitive]]. If the relation is also [[reflexive relation|reflexive]], then the relation is an [[equivalence relation]].

== Definition ==

Formally, a relation <math>R</math> on a set <math>X</math> is a PER if it holds for all <math>a, b, c \in X</math> that:

# if <math>a R b</math>, then <math>b R a</math> (symmetry)
# if <math>a R b</math> and <math>b R c</math>, then <math>a R c</math> (transitivity)

Another definition for a partial equivalence relation is that <math>R</math> on a set <math>X</math> is a PER if there is some subset <math>Y</math> of <math>X</math> such that <math>R \subseteq Y \times Y</math> and <math>R</math> is an [[equivalence relation]] on <math>Y</math>. The two definitions are seen to be equivalent by taking <math>Y = \{ x \in X \mid x\,R\,x\}</math>.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Mitchell |first1=John C. |title=Foundations for programming languages |date=1996 |publisher=MIT Press |location=Cambridge, Mass. |isbn=0585037892 |pages=364–365}}</ref>

== Properties and applications ==

The following properties hold for a partial equivalence relation <math>R</math> on a set <math>X</math>:

* <math>R</math> is an equivalence relation on the subset <math>Y = \{ x \in X \mid x\,R\,x\} \subseteq X</math>.<ref group=note>By construction, <math>R</math> is reflexive on <math>Y</math> and therefore an equivalence relation on <math>Y</math>.</ref>
* <math>R</math> is [[difunctional relation|difunctional]]: the relation is the set <math>\{(a,b) \mid f a = g b \}</math> for two [[partial function]]s <math>f,g : X \rightharpoonup Y</math> and some indicator set <math>Y</math>
* <math>R</math> is right [[Euclidean relation|Euclidean]]: For <math>a,b,c \in X</math>, <math>a R b</math> and <math>a R c</math> implies <math>b R c</math>
* <math>R</math> is left Euclidean: For <math>a,b,c \in X</math>, <math>b R a</math> and <math>c R a</math> imply <math>b R c</math>
* <math>R</math> is [[quasi-reflexive relation|quasi-reflexive]]: If <math>x, y \in X</math> and <math>x R y</math>, then <math>x R x</math> and <math>y R y</math>.<ref>[https://www.britannica.com/topic/formal-logic/Logical-manipulations-in-LPC#ref534730 Encyclopaedia Britannica] (EB); although EB's notion of quasi-reflexivity is Wikipedia's notion of left quasi-reflexivity, they coincide for symmetric relations.</ref><ref group=note>This follows since if <math>x R y</math>, then <math>y R x</math> by symmetry, so <math>x R x</math> and <math>y R y</math> by transitivity. It is also a consequence of the Euclidean properties.</ref>

None of these properties alone is sufficient to imply that the relation is a PER.<ref group=note>For the equivalence relation, consider the set <math>E=\{a,b,c,d\}</math> and the relation <math>R=\{a,b,c\}^2\cup\{(d,a)\}</math>. <math>R</math> is an equivalence relation on <math>\{a,b,c\}</math> but not a PER on <math>E</math> since it is neither symmetric (<math>dRa</math>, but not <math>aRd</math>) nor transitive (<math>dRa</math> and <math>aRb</math>, but not <math>dRb</math>). For Euclideanness (and quasi-reflexivity), ''xRy'' on natural numbers, defined by 0 ≤ ''x'' ≤ ''y''+1 ≤ 2, is right Euclidean (and hence quasi-reflexive), but neither symmetric (since e.g. 2''R''1, but not 1''R''2) nor transitive (since e.g. 2''R''1 and 1''R''0, but not 2''R''0).</ref> If <math>R</math> is both left ''and'' right Euclidean, then <math>R</math> is an equivalence relation, and hence a PER.

===In non-set-theory settings===

In [[type theory]], [[constructive mathematics]] and their applications to [[computer science]], constructing analogues of subsets is often problematic<ref>{{Cite book|chapter-url=https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/5135|doi=10.1109/LICS.1988.5135|chapter=The strength of the subset type in Martin-Lof's type theory|title=&#91;1988&#93; Proceedings. Third Annual Information Symposium on Logic in Computer Science|year=1988|last1=Salveson|first1=A.|last2=Smith|first2=J.M.|pages=384–391|isbn=0-8186-0853-6|s2cid=15822016}}</ref>—in these contexts PERs are therefore more commonly used, particularly to define [[setoid]]s, sometimes called partial setoids. Forming a partial setoid from a type and a PER is analogous to forming subsets and quotients in classical set-theoretic mathematics.

The algebraic notion of [[Congruence relation|congruence]] can also be generalized to partial equivalences, yielding the notion of [[subcongruence]], i.e. a [[homomorphic relation]] that is symmetric and transitive, but not necessarily reflexive.<ref>{{cite book|editor1=Aldo Ursini |editor2=Paulo Agliano|title=Logic and Algebra|year=1996|publisher=CRC Press|isbn=978-0-8247-9606-8|pages=161–180|author=J. Lambek|chapter=The Butterfly and the Serpent}}</ref>

==Examples==

A simple example of a PER that is ''not'' an equivalence relation is the [[empty relation]] <math>R=\emptyset</math>, if <math>X</math> is not empty.

===Kernels of partial functions===
If <math>f</math> is a [[partial function]] on a set <math>A</math>, then the relation <math>\approx</math> defined by 
: <math>x \approx y</math> if <math>f</math> is defined at <math>x</math>, <math>f</math> is defined at <math>y</math>, and <math>f(x) = f(y)</math>
is a partial equivalence relation, since it is clearly symmetric and transitive.

If <math>f</math> is undefined on some elements, then <math>\approx</math> is not an equivalence relation. It is not reflexive since if <math>f(x)</math> is not defined then <math>x \not\approx x</math> &mdash; in fact, for such an <math>x</math> there is no <math>y \in A</math> such that <math>x \approx y</math>.  It follows immediately that the largest subset of <math>A</math> on which <math>\approx</math> is an equivalence relation is precisely the subset on which <math>f</math> is defined.

===Functions respecting equivalence relations===
Let ''X'' and ''Y'' be sets equipped with equivalence relations (or PERs) <math>\approx_X, \approx_Y</math>. For <math>f,g : X \to Y</math>, define <math>f \approx g</math> to mean:

: <math>\forall x_0 \; x_1, \quad x_0 \approx_X x_1 \Rightarrow f(x_0) \approx_Y g(x_1)</math>

then <math>f \approx f</math> means that ''f'' induces a well-defined function of the quotients <math>X / {\approx_X} \; \to \; Y / {\approx_Y}</math>. Thus, the PER <math>\approx</math> captures both the idea of ''definedness'' on the quotients and of two functions inducing the same function on the quotient.

===Equality of IEEE floating point values===
The [[IEEE 754|IEEE 754:2008]] standard for [[floating-point numbers]] defines an "EQ" relation for floating point values. This predicate is symmetric and transitive, but is not reflexive because of the presence of [[NaN]] values that are not EQ to themselves.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Goldberg | first = David
 | doi = 10.1145/103162.103163
 | issue = 1
 | journal = ACM Computing Surveys
 | pages = 5–48
 | title = What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic
 | volume = 23
 | year = 1991}} See page 33.</ref>
